title: Our Ancient Ancestors’ Lost Habitat Revealed by 700,000-Year-Old Elephant’s Tooth - Nautilus

text: Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisementPaleontologyOur Ancient Ancestors’ Lost Habitat Revealed by 700,000-Year-Old Elephant’s ToothAn elephant’s tooth never forgetsJCBy Jake Currie5:00 PM CDT on October 8, 2026Add Nautilus to GoogleThe Levant was a busy corridor around a million years ago. Long before it became a place where modern humans and Neanderthals mingled, the narrow land bridge linking Africa to Eurasia proved to be a popular thoroughfare for other ancient hominins who settled in the region (most likely Homo erectus and Homo heidelbergensis). Unfortunately, there’s still a lot we don’t know about the paleoclimate there, but we recently got some clues thanks to an elephant’s tooth.The tooth, dated to around 700,000 years ago, was discovered alongside tusk fragments and a cache of basalt hand axes from the same period in the Daughters of Jacob Bridge region just south of Israel’s Hula Valley. A research team led by archaeologists from Haifa University performed some high-tech dentistry on the tooth, employing CT scans, 3D construction, and isotopic analysis, and recently published their results in Quaternary Science Reviews.  Read more: “Here’s What the Whiskers on an Elephant’s Trunk Do”Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisement
